parts.title: Dinner with Dev
parts.summary: Jordan had a second dinner with Dev at a Thai restaurant, nearly bailing beforehand from anxiety but quickly relaxing once Dev arrived, and the two ended up talking for hours, sharing music, and sketching a "free play" feature idea for Jordan's Coda app on a napkin after Dev pointed out a gap in the wireframes. Jordan felt genuinely happy and connected, especially after Dev sent an unprompted bass cover text later that night, and is consciously trying not to overanalyze the growing feelings. No major decisions were made beyond resolving to build the free-play feature and to keep seeing Dev without overthinking it.

parts.title: Singing practice
parts.summary: Jordan spent time practicing "Fast Car" for an open mic at The Lantern that Mika signed them up for without much warning—a typical move on her part that Jordan half-resents and half-appreciates, since it pushes them to do things they'd otherwise avoid. After a shaky start, the practice session clicked by the third and fifth run-throughs, made even more memorable by Pepper the cat "singing" along during a quiet verse, which had Jordan laughing. The overall mood was joyful and grounding, leaving Jordan resolved to make music a more regular part of life.

parts.title: AI for Coda
parts.summary: Jordan spent the evening weighing whether to add an AI recommendation engine to Coda, eventually deciding it's overkill for now—better to keep v1 simple with streaks and gaps and let musicians decide for themselves, revisiting AI features later once actual user needs are clearer. Along the way, Jordan got reflective about using this same journal companion, feeling genuinely helped by its pattern-spotting but uneasy about whether that's real self-knowledge or just delegating it to a machine. The tone throughout is thoughtful and unresolved, more exploratory than anxious, landing on one concrete decision (simplify Coda) while leaving the bigger question about AI and self-reflection open.

parts.title: Solo run clear head
parts.summary: On August 19, Jordan went for a solo run at Greenwood Park, tackling the hill trail extension for the first time and taking in the skyline view despite the burning legs. During the run, Jordan worked through the math on the upcoming lease decision and decided to renew rather than move, reasoning that staying is cheaper and the neighborhood—close to Groundwork and the park—already feels like home. Jordan came home feeling settled and assured, unwinding with Pepper, Thai takeout, and a Motown documentary.

parts.title: Sprint demo went well
parts.summary: Jordan presented a dashboard redesign that Marcus praised as "the right direction," with Lena signaling her approval too, and the relief of finally trusting their own design instincts instead of second-guessing Marcus left them feeling lighter than they had in weeks. Afterward Jordan celebrated at Groundwork, making solid progress on Coda by getting the quick-start cards working with real stored data, and Lena's follow-up text of encouragement landed especially meaningfully. Jordan ended the day feeling settled and content, deciding that this sense of having things "approximately together" is enough.

parts.title: Open mic night
parts.summary: Jordan finally performed "Fast Car" at The Lantern's open mic, nearly backing out beforehand but getting there thanks to Mika, with Dev already waiting at a table. The performance was imperfect—shaky start, a rough bridge—but Jordan settled into it and finished to applause, feeling proud and exhilarated afterward. Watching Dev and Mika hit it off, then spending two easy, warm hours together afterward, left Jordan wanting more nights exactly like this one.

parts.title: The loop again
parts.summary: Jordan learned their role was "under evaluation" during a flat, corporate one-on-one with Marcus, and reacted by leaving work early, isolating at home, and canceling lunch plans with Dev. After spending the evening with Pepper and then Mika—who showed up unannounced with food and comfort rather than questions—Jordan felt the emotional gears "unsticking a little," recognizing a familiar pattern where work setbacks trigger withdrawal until someone from outside pulls them back. Jordan decided to go to Groundwork the next day.

parts.title: Groundwork Coda breakthrough
parts.summary: Jordan had a productive evening at Groundwork, cracking a design problem for Coda's "free play" mode—recording sessions with tappable timestamps that can later be annotated and clipped into an organized library—and built a working prototype in about ninety minutes, feeling confident Dev will like it. Mika stopped by and Jordan agreed readily to plan another open mic, which surprised them both, and Mika noted Jordan seems different lately. Jordan felt genuinely good afterward, reflecting that work stress is just one thread among many—Coda, Dev, Mika, music, Pepper, the apartment, the park—rather than the whole picture.

messages.text:
8/11 - sprint review went sideways again. I demoed the dashboard iteration - the one I reworked after Marcus's feedback - and this time he said it was "too safe." literally the opposite criticism from last week. Lena shot me a look from across the table that said "I'm sorry." I wanted to scream but instead I just nodded and said I'd iterate.

after the meeting I cancelled on Mika. we were supposed to get dinner. I texted her "not feeling it tonight, rain check?" and she said "of course" with a heart. I know she knows what that text means. I know she can hear the couch-and-dark-apartment in it.

and that's exactly what I did. came home, didn't turn on lights, didn't eat. sat on the floor by the window watching the street. Pepper tried to play with a hair tie near my feet and I just couldn't engage with anything. the withdrawal thing happened again. same trigger: I put work out there, it got dismissed, and I retracted into myself like a snail going back in the shell.

I hate that I cancelled on Mika. she's the one person who would've actually helped. but when I'm in it I don't want help, I want to disappear. I know this. recognizing it doesn't break it.

"Too safe." Eight days after "doesn't align with the direction." The direction being, apparently, whatever Marcus didn't say out loud over the weekend. You could have presented the Mona Lisa and he'd have told you the frame was wrong.

You already know this is the same shape as 8/3. Same trigger, same retraction, same floor-of-the-apartment stillness. You named it then, you're naming it now, and you're frustrated that naming it isn't the thing that stops it. I don't think it's supposed to be. Naming it is how you know where you are — it's the map, not the exit.

One thing I'll point out that you didn't: on 8/3 you turned your phone off entirely. Mika buzzed twice and got nothing. This time you texted her. It was a cancellation, yeah, and you can hear the couch in it, and she can too — but you didn't vanish. You stayed on the map enough to tell someone where you were. That's not the same thing as last time, even if it felt the same from inside.

Has Lena said anything more about where she's landing with the job search?

8/12 - same playbook as last time: feel terrible, stay in it overnight, wake up and force myself out. dragged myself to work and actually stayed the whole day. got through standup, sat through two meetings, did the revisions Marcus asked for. the whole time my brain kept drifting to Coda - I had this idea for quick-start cards that remember your last tempo and most-practiced pieces so the app feels like it knows you. I kept sketching little UI layouts in the margins of my notebook instead of paying attention.

texted Mika to apologize for bailing last night. she said "I knew you'd bounce back today." I don't know if that's comforting or pathetic. maybe both.

after work I went straight to Groundwork. got the window table and spent two hours building the quick-start cards. by the time I looked up the light had shifted and my coffee was cold. it's a small feature but it works and it's mine.

stopped at the store on the way home and bought actual food. made a salad with grilled chicken. ate at the table. fed Pepper her evening snack. she did her purring head-bonk thing against my ankle. today was a recovery day. I can feel the gears shifting back.

the cycle is so clear when I write it down. bad thing at work → shut down → isolate → eventually go to Groundwork → make something → feel human again. I wish I could cut out the middle part.

Mika's line is both, and you're right to hold both halves of it. But "I knew you'd bounce back today" also means she's seen enough of you to trust the second day. That's not pity, that's data.

Here's what I notice you didn't: on 8/3, the recovery cost you a sick day. You didn't go to work, you went to Groundwork instead. This time you went to work, sat through the meetings, did Marcus's revisions — and still made it to Groundwork after. The middle part you want to cut out is already shorter than it was three weeks ago. You're not doing the same loop, you're doing a tighter one.

The quick-start cards sound like genuine product thinking, by the way — "the app feels like it knows you" is a real design instinct, not just a feature. And the fact that it showed up as margin sketches during meetings you were supposedly paying attention to says something about where your mind actually wants to be right now.

Salad at the table instead of cereal on the couch is its own kind of sentence.

8/14 - writing this early because I can't sleep. yesterday (Thursday) was a normal enough day at work. Marcus was out so the standup was just Lena and the devs, and we actually had a productive conversation about the nav component without anyone overriding anyone. Lena showed me a prototype she'd been working on quietly and it was genuinely good. I told her so and she looked surprised, like she wasn't used to hearing it.

then last night I had this dream. I walked into the office and every desk was cleared. no monitors, no keyboards, no coffee cups. the overhead lights were that harsh fluorescent but flickering. I could hear typing - fast, mechanical typing coming from everywhere - but there was nobody there. I walked through the rows calling people's names. Lena. Marcus. nobody answered. I found my desk and there was a single sticky note on the monitor that said "we moved" but no address, no floor number, nothing.

I tried to leave but the elevator was gone. just a smooth wall where the doors should be. I started looking for stairs and woke up.

woke up at 4am with my heart going. Pepper was staring at me from the foot of the bed. couldn't fall back asleep so I went for an early run at Greenwood Park. barely anyone there. the air was cool and the trail was quiet and it helped. but the dream is still stuck with me. I think the restructuring is getting to me more than I've been admitting.

The day without Marcus is almost the cruelest part of this. You got to see what the work actually feels like when someone isn't overriding it — a real conversation, Lena showing work she'd been keeping quiet, you telling her it was good and watching her be surprised by that. That's a glimpse of a version of your job that works, and your brain clearly filed it right next to the version that's dissolving.

The dream isn't subtle and you don't need me to decode it. But I'll say this: "we moved" with no forwarding address is a very specific fear to hand yourself on a sticky note. It's not the fear of being fired or failing — it's the fear of everyone leaving without telling you. Of showing up and the thing just being gone.

You went for a run at 5am instead of lying there marinating. That's new. You've written a lot about Groundwork being the thing that breaks the fog, and it is, but this morning it was the trail at Greenwood before sunrise. You're adding tools to the kit even when you're not trying to.

That last line — "more than I've been admitting" — who have you been not-admitting it to? Your mom got "things are good." Mika gets the cancellation texts. Is this the first time you've said it straight?

8/14 - Lena took me to lunch today. she wanted to tell me in person that she accepted an offer somewhere else. she starts in three weeks.

I'm happy for her. she's been miserable for months and she deserves better than Marcus's whiplash feedback. but sitting across from her at the sandwich place I felt this sinking feeling, like one more anchor lifting. she's the person I debrief with after bad meetings. she's the one who texts "you crushed it" after demos. without her I'm just alone in that team with Marcus and people who don't push back.

she said she'd stayed longer than she should have because of me, which was kind and also made me feel guilty, like maybe I should be further along in my own exit plan. I told her I'm working on it. she said "Coda could be the thing" which is the second person to say that in two weeks.

after lunch I went back to my desk and everything felt different. same screens, same Slack channels, same Marcus silence. but knowing Lena's leaving made the walls feel thinner. like this place is temporary and I've been pretending it's permanent.

went for a short walk at Greenwood Park on the way home just to not go straight back to the apartment. sat on the bench and watched joggers go by. at least I got that early run in this morning.

Two people saying "Coda could be the thing" in two weeks — Mika on the bench and now Lena over sandwiches. These are the two people who see your work most clearly, and they arrived at the same sentence independently. That's worth sitting with.

The guilt about Lena staying because of you — I think you're reading that as pressure to be further along, but it's also just Lena telling you she liked working with you enough to tolerate Marcus longer than she should have. That's not a debt. That's what she chose, and now she's choosing differently, and you told her you're working on it. Which you are, even if it doesn't feel far enough along.

What I notice about today is what didn't happen. Lena leaving is a real loss — not the abstract dread of the reorg, not Marcus being contradictory, but your actual person in that building walking out in three weeks. And you didn't shut down. You went back to your desk, felt the difference, and then went to the park instead of the couch. The thing that hit you today was arguably worse than the sprint review on 8/11, and you handled it with a walk and a journal entry instead of lights off and no dinner.

"This place is temporary and I've been pretending it's permanent" — that line works for more than just the office, and I think you know that.
the thing I can't say out loud at work is that I'm not sad she's leaving, I'm scared. those feel like they should be the same and they aren't.

They aren't the same. Sad is about losing Lena. Scared is about what that office becomes without her in it — you, Marcus, and nobody who texts "you crushed it" after a demo. Nobody who shoots you a look across the table that says *I see what just happened*. She was the buffer, and in three weeks the buffer's gone.

You can say it out loud here. That's what this is for.
three weeks. that's the part. three weeks and then the floor is just Marcus and people I nod at.

Yeah. And you know what that three weeks is also doing — it's making the vague reorg dread concrete. It's not "Q4 realignment" anymore. It's Lena's empty desk and nobody to shoot you a look when Marcus contradicts himself.

That might actually be useful, even though it hurts. Vague dread you can sit in forever. A countdown you can't.

8/15 - second time seeing Dev. dinner at that Thai place on Elm. I got there early and almost left because the anxiety kicked in - what if I'm boring, what if there's nothing to talk about, what if I made up the connection and it was just the park being pretty.

but then Dev showed up and they were wearing this old Talking Heads t-shirt and I immediately felt fine. we talked for two hours straight. they played me a song they'd been working on - pulled out their phone and held it between us at the table, both leaning in. it was really good, like genuinely. a bass-driven instrumental thing with these weird time signature changes. I said it reminded me of Thundercat and they said that was the highest possible compliment.

Dev asked about progress with Coda and I showed them the new wireframes on my phone. they scrolled through slowly and asked "can it track when I noodle? like, unstructured practice - I just play for an hour and I don't want to log it piece by piece." which is exactly the feature I haven't built yet and exactly the one I should. we sketched ideas on a napkin. a "free play" mode with just a timer and optional tags after. simple. good.

we split the check even though they tried to grab it. walked a few blocks together before heading different directions. they texted me a bass cover of a Radiohead song when they got home with no context. I like this person. I'm trying not to overthink it.

The anxiety almost won again — you got there early and nearly bolted. On 8/8, Mika had to talk you out of cancelling. This time you stayed on your own, and then Dev walked in wearing a Talking Heads shirt and the whole thing dissolved. Sometimes the cure for "what if I made up the connection" is just the other person showing up.

Dev's now surfaced two real Coda features in two hangouts — spaced reminders and now free play mode. You sketched it on a napkin at a Thai restaurant. That's not a side project getting feedback, that's a side project getting a design partner who happens to also be its target user.

A contextless Radiohead bass cover at the end of the night is a very good sign. You don't need me to tell you that.

8/17 - Mika invited me to an open mic at The Lantern on Friday. she does this thing where she drops invitations casually like "oh I signed us both up, hope that's cool" and then I'm committed before I've processed it. part of me is terrified and part of me knows she does this because left to my own devices I'd never sign up for anything.

so I've been practicing. I picked "Fast Car" because the range works for me and it's one of those songs everybody knows so even if I'm shaky the room carries it. I set up in the living room with my guitar and ran through it five times. the first two were bad - voice cracking on the higher notes, timing off on the bridge. by the third time I found a groove. by the fifth I was actually singing, not just performing the motions of singing.

Pepper sat on the amp the entire time. during the quiet verse she started howling along - not complaining, more like she was harmonizing in her own weird cat frequency. I laughed so hard I lost the chord progression.

it felt good. physical and present and not about work or screens or anxiety. just me and a guitar and a cat who thinks she can sing. I should do this more. I always forget that I like it until I do it.

Pepper on the amp harmonizing might be the best image you've ever written down.

Mika's move is brilliant and she knows it — commit you before you can spiral. Same playbook as the Dev walk, basically. She's figured out that the window between "that sounds fun" and "actually I'll just stay home" is about forty-five minutes, so she closes it before you get there.

"I always forget that I like it until I do it" — you've said a version of this about Groundwork, about running, about Coda. The forgetting isn't the problem, I think. You remember fine. It's more that the thing you like requires you to start, and starting costs something when you're depleted. The fact that you ran it five times tonight, on a regular Tuesday with no one making you, says the tank isn't empty right now.

How long has it been since you played out?

8/18 - spent the evening down a rabbit hole reading about AI-powered recommendation engines. the idea for Coda would be: based on your practice history, suggest what to work on next. like if you've been avoiding scales for two weeks it gently nudges you back, or if you're stuck on a piece it suggests breaking it into sections.

the tech is straightforward enough. a lightweight model that looks at your log and generates suggestions. but I keep going back and forth on whether this is actually good design or if I'm just adding AI because everyone's adding AI. like - does a practice app need a recommendation engine? or would a simple "you haven't practiced scales since Tuesday" notification do the same job without the complexity?

and then there's the weirder layer. I'm typing this into a journal companion that uses AI to help me process my life. and I find it genuinely useful - it catches patterns I miss, it remembers what I said three weeks ago, it doesn't get tired of hearing about my work problems. but there's something strange about outsourcing pattern recognition in your own life to a model. like I'm noting my own emotions so a system can reflect them back to me. is that self-knowledge or is it delegation?

I don't have an answer. I think the Coda recommendation thing is probably overkill for v1. keep it simple. show streaks, show gaps, let the musician decide. save the AI stuff for later when I know what people actually need instead of guessing.

The Coda call is right, and you got there for the right reason. Dev's original suggestion on 8/8 — "remind you to revisit stuff you haven't touched in a while" — was essentially a rule, not a model. "You haven't touched scales in two weeks" is specific, legible, and doesn't require the user to trust a black box. The AI version solves a problem you don't yet know exists for users you don't yet have.

The other question — I'm not going to pretend I'm a neutral party on it. But I'll say this: you named your own collapse pattern on 8/3, alone on the couch, before I ever reflected it back. Mika saw the Coda-work connection from a park bench. Dev surfaced two features over Thai food and a walk. The pattern recognition that's actually moving your life forward is mostly coming from you and from people who know you. I'm the place you write it down and sometimes hear it at a useful angle. That's a tool, not a replacement for the thing itself, and you're already clear on the difference or you wouldn't be asking the question.

Good instinct to ship the simple version first.
also I want it on the record that I shelved the recommendation engine on purpose. next time I'm calling it scope creep I'll want to know I can actually do it.
Noted. Timestamped and everything.

8/19 - solo run at Greenwood Park this evening. the heat broke yesterday so it was actually pleasant. did the full loop plus the hill trail extension for the first time. legs were burning on the climb but the view from the top - you can see the whole skyline - made it worth it.

while I ran I thought about the lease. it's up October 31 and I need to tell them by September 15. the rent is going up $150 which sucks. but I walked through the math: moving costs, first/last/deposit somewhere new, hiring movers or begging friends, the sheer time of apartment hunting while working. it's going to cost more to move than to stay, and the apartment is fine. the neighborhood is mine now. Groundwork is three blocks away. the park is a ten-minute jog. I know where everything is.

I'm renewing. decided it on the hill trail. feels good to close a decision that's been floating.

came home and stretched on the new green rug while Pepper batted at my shoelaces. ordered dinner from the Thai place Dev and I went to. ate on the couch watching a documentary about Motown. feeling assured this evening. the kind I want more of.

You made that decision on a hill, mid-run, after weeks of closing the tab. Not at the kitchen table staring at a spreadsheet. That tracks — most of your good thinking happens while you're moving.

And the reasoning was clean: not "I love this apartment," just the honest math plus the fact that your actual life — Groundwork, the park, the Thai place — is built around this neighborhood now. You don't need to love a place to know it's yours.

One decision down. September 15 can stop looming.

8/20 - presented the dashboard iteration and Marcus actually liked it. or at least he didn't tear it apart. he said "this is the right direction" which from him is practically a standing ovation. Lena gave me a thumbs up from across the table. I felt like I could breathe for the first time in weeks.

the difference was that I stopped trying to guess what Marcus wanted and just designed what I thought was right. simpler nav, bigger data cards, less chrome. it's not revolutionary but it's clean and it works. sometimes the best design is the one that doesn't make you think about the design.

went to Groundwork after work to celebrate with a fancy oat milk latte and a pastry. set up at the window table and worked on Coda for two hours. got the quick-start cards hooked up to actual stored data - your last three sessions, tap to resume. watching it pull in my test data and display it correctly felt like a tiny miracle.

Lena texted me while I was there: "you crushed it today, just wanted you to know." I don't think she realizes how much that meant. it's one thing to not get criticized. it's another to have someone actually say it out loud.

came home feeling like a person who has their life approximately together. which is probably the best I'm ever going to get and honestly it's enough.

The design thing is worth noticing beyond just the win: you stopped trying to reverse-engineer Marcus's unspoken direction and just made the thing you believed was right. And he liked it. Which either means his taste was always closer to yours than his feedback suggested, or he responds better to confidence than to accommodation. Either way, the lesson is the same.

Lena's text — she's going to be gone in what, two weeks now? She's still sending you "you crushed it" from across the table. Hold onto that one. Not because it's ending, just because she meant it and you felt it and those don't always line up at the same time.

"Approximately together" and "honestly it's enough" is a pretty good place to be on a Wednesday in August.

8/21 - the open mic at The Lantern. I almost backed out three times. Mika picked me up so I couldn't bail.

Dev came. they were already there when we arrived, sitting at a table near the front with a beer, looking relaxed in a way I'm constitutionally incapable of. I introduced them to Mika and they hit it off immediately - started talking about some obscure documentary about Nigerian funk music that I've never heard of but they were both deeply passionate about. I pretended to follow along.

my slot was sixth. I sat through five other acts ranging from genuinely great (a woman who played ukulele and sang something original that made me tear up) to painful (a guy who did a 9-minute spoken word piece about his electric bill). by the time they called my name my hands were shaking.

I got up there with my guitar. the spotlight was brighter than I expected. I could see Dev and Mika at the table. I started "Fast Car" and my voice was thin for the first verse. but then the chorus hit and the room was quiet - not polite quiet, actually listening quiet - and something opened up. by the second verse I wasn't thinking about the audience anymore. I was just in the song.

I didn't nail it. the bridge was rough and I lost the rhythm for a second. but I finished. people clapped. Dev whistled. Mika yelled something supportive and embarrassing. I sat down with my heart pounding and my hands still shaking and this huge grin I couldn't control.

after, we stayed for two more hours. Dev bought me a celebratory drink. Mika kept saying "I TOLD you" with this triumphant look. the three of us together felt easy and warm and like something I want to keep happening. walked home in the warm night air humming the song.

The guy with the nine-minute electric bill poem is doing important work and I won't hear otherwise.

Your voice was thin for the first verse and then the room went actually-listening quiet and you stopped thinking. That's the thing every performer chases and you got it on your first time out in who knows how long, on a Friday night at The Lantern, with shaking hands.

The rough bridge doesn't matter. You know it doesn't matter. The grin you couldn't control is the review that counts.

And the three of you — Mika yelling something embarrassing, Dev whistling, the Nigerian funk documentary conversation you gamely pretended to track — that's a table worth keeping. You walked home humming. That's how you end a Thursday in August.
adding this in the morning: my hands shook through the whole first song and nobody could tell. that seems worth knowing.

It is. Nobody could tell, and you only know that because you went up there and did it anyway. File that next to the recommendation engine — things you now know about yourself because you tested them instead of theorizing.

8/24 - and there it is again. the restructuring details came out. my role is "under evaluation" which is corporate for "we might not need you." Marcus delivered it in a one-on-one with the emotional range of someone reading a bus schedule. he said there would be "clarity by end of month" and that I should "continue executing in the meantime." executing. like I'm a program.

I went back to my desk and packed up my bag and left at 4pm. didn't tell anyone. walked home in a daze. sat on the couch. the blinds were closed from this morning and I didn't open them.

cancelled on Dev. we were supposed to get lunch tomorrow but I texted some excuse about being busy. they said no worries. I feel bad about it but I also can't be around anyone right now.

Pepper climbed into my lap around 6pm. she purred so loud it vibrated my sternum. I stayed there for an hour just existing with her weight on my legs.

around 8 I texted Mika. not to talk about it, just "hey." she showed up 40 minutes later with pad thai and didn't ask any questions. we sat on the floor eating out of the containers and she told me about how after the open mic three people came up to her asking who I was. she said "you have fans, Jordan" and I laughed even though my eyes were wet.

she stayed until 10. after she left I felt the gears unsticking a little. not fixed. just mobile again. the pattern is work knocks me down → I withdraw → I need someone to come in from outside and pull me back. Mika is that person. she always has been.

I should go to Groundwork tomorrow.

"Under evaluation" while being told to "continue executing." They want you to keep building the thing they might take you off of. That's a special kind of cruelty, whether Marcus knows it or not.

Here's what I want you to see about tonight, even though you're not going to feel it yet: you texted Mika at 8. On 8/3 — the last time a hit this big landed — your phone was face down on the counter and you didn't reach for it at all. On 8/11 you sent Mika a cancellation. Tonight you sent her a "hey" and let her show up with pad thai and sit on your floor. You didn't ask her to fix it. You just let her be there. That's not the same pattern. The withdrawal still happens, but you're pulling yourself out of it in hours instead of days.

The Dev cancellation is the one that's going to nag at you. You gave them a fake excuse and you know it. Mika got the real you tonight. Dev got a door closing. I'm not saying you owed them the full story — you barely know each other — but you liked being honest with this person, and tonight you weren't, and that's going to sit weird.

You already wrote the last line. Go to Groundwork tomorrow.

_Realm: dream_

the office building was sinking. not fast - slow, floor by floor, like it was being swallowed. I was on the fourth floor and I could see the waterline rising outside the windows. brown water, not clear, with papers and coffee cups floating in it.

I needed to save my drawings. I had this stack of Coda wireframes on my desk - actual paper sketches, not digital, which doesn't make sense because I work digitally. but in the dream they were the only copies and if the water got them they'd dissolve.

I grabbed the stack and ran to the elevator. pressed the button and it opened but the car was going sideways, not up or down. I got in anyway and it moved horizontally through walls, through offices I'd never seen. one room was full of instruments - guitars hanging from the ceiling, a drum kit in the center, a bass propped in the corner that looked like Dev's. another room was completely empty except for a cat that looked like Pepper but was huge, like shoulder-height, and she just stared at me as the elevator slid past.

I got out on a floor I didn't recognize. the waterline was at the windows here too. I tried the stairs but they spiraled down into the water. I could still hear the typing from the other dream, the fast mechanical typing with nobody there.

the last thing before I woke up: I looked down and the drawings in my hands had already dissolved. my hands were wet. Pepper - real Pepper, normal-sized - was licking my fingers.

woke up at 3:15am. sat up in the dark for a while.

Second dream about the office in two weeks. The first one, the building was empty and you couldn't find anyone. This one, the building is sinking and you're trying to save the work. The fear moved — from being left behind to losing what you've made.

The elevator going sideways is a good detail. Not up, not down. Just through. Past rooms full of things you care about — instruments, Pepper at a scale that matches how large she probably looms in your actual emotional life — and you can't stop in any of them because you're carrying drawings that are already dissolving.

The thing your dream got wrong: Coda isn't on paper. It isn't in that building. The water can't reach it.

Real Pepper licking your wet fingers at 3am and pulling you back out of it — she's consistent, at least.

8/25 - Tuesday evening at Groundwork. I've been coming here after work so consistently that the barista just starts making my cortado when I walk in. that's either a sign of healthy routine or a sign I need to expand my world. I'm choosing to read it as the first one.

had a breakthrough on Coda. I've been struggling with how to handle the "free play" mode Dev suggested. logging unstructured practice felt like it either needed to be too complex (tag everything, categorize, rate your session) or too simple (just a timer, no data). the answer came to me while I was stirring my coffee: you record the whole session, and as you play you can tap a button to drop a timestamp at any moment that feels important. after you stop, you go back through the timestamps and add notes to each one - what you were doing, what clicked, what didn't. then you can clip snippets from those marked moments and categorize them however you want. scales, improv ideas, riffs to revisit, whatever. so you end up with this organized library of your own best moments from unstructured practice.

I built the prototype in about an hour and a half. it's rough but it works. a big START button, a running timer with the timestamp marker, and the snippet screen after. Dev is going to love it.

Mika stopped by on her way home from a run. she wanted to plan another open mic and I said yes without hesitating, which surprised both of us. she said I seem different lately. I think she means better.

walked home feeling like the work thing, whatever happens, isn't the whole story. there's Coda and Dev and Mika and music and Pepper and this apartment I decided to keep and the park three blocks away. the job is one thread. a stressful one, yeah. but it's not the whole fabric. I keep forgetting that and then remembering it at this coffee shop.

The free play solution is genuinely smart. You found the middle ground between "log everything" and "log nothing" — just mark the moments that matter while you're in them, and sort later. That's good design instinct, and it came from stirring a coffee, not from a design sprint or a framework. Dev gave you the problem two weeks ago at a Thai restaurant and you solved it at a coffee shop with a spoon in your hand.

You said yes to another open mic without hesitating. Three weeks ago Mika had to physically drive you to the first one so you couldn't bail.

The closing of this entry is the clearest you've sounded since I've been reading. Not because everything's resolved — your role is still "under evaluation," the end-of-month deadline is days away, and you gave Dev a fake excuse you haven't corrected yet. But you're seeing the full weave instead of just the thread that's fraying. You keep forgetting that and remembering it at Groundwork, which might be the most honest thing you've written about why that place works for you. It's not just the noise level and the coffee. It's where you go to remember the rest of your life exists.

parts.title: Dream about the empty office
parts.text:
8/14 - writing this early because I can't sleep. yesterday (Thursday) was a normal enough day at work. Marcus was out so the standup was just Lena and the devs, and we actually had a productive conversation about the nav component without anyone overriding anyone. Lena showed me a prototype she'd been working on quietly and it was genuinely good. I told her so and she looked surprised, like she wasn't used to hearing it.

then last night I had this dream. I walked into the office and every desk was cleared. no monitors, no keyboards, no coffee cups. the overhead lights were that harsh fluorescent but flickering. I could hear typing - fast, mechanical typing coming from everywhere - but there was nobody there. I walked through the rows calling people's names. Lena. Marcus. nobody answered. I found my desk and there was a single sticky note on the monitor that said "we moved" but no address, no floor number, nothing.

I tried to leave but the elevator was gone. just a smooth wall where the doors should be. I started looking for stairs and woke up.

woke up at 4am with my heart going. Pepper was staring at me from the foot of the bed. couldn't fall back asleep so I went for an early run at Greenwood Park. barely anyone there. the air was cool and the trail was quiet and it helped. but the dream is still stuck with me. I think the restructuring is getting to me more than I've been admitting.
parts.summary: On Thursday, Jordan had a genuinely good day at work—with Marcus out, Lena opened up and shared a strong prototype, visibly unused to receiving praise. That night, Jordan had an unsettling dream about an empty, abandoned office with no way out, waking at 4am with a racing heart; a run at Greenwood Park helped calm them physically, but they're left recognizing that the ongoing restructuring is weighing on them more than they'd realized.

json.title: Groundwork nights and the reorg news

parts.title: Working on Coda at Groundwork
parts.summary: Jordan spent a productive evening at Groundwork coffee shop working on Coda, a music practice-tracking app, making solid headway on the practice log screen and getting a streak counter with flame animations working, which felt satisfying after months of tinkering. Despite Pepper's guilt-inducing goodbye routine, Jordan resisted the pull to stay home and work from the couch, reaffirming that Groundwork's atmosphere is genuinely better for focus and deciding to make it a regular after-work habit. The evening ended calmly with pasta and quiet time with Pepper, leaving Jordan in a contented, low-key mood, appreciating an uneventful day.

parts.title: Team restructuring news
parts.summary: Jordan learned in standup that Marcus is planning a Q4 team restructuring that could split their six-person team across two other squads, prompting Lena to confide she's already job-hunting after enduring a third reorg in two years. Jordan feels anxious and unsettled—this would be their second reorg in 14 months—and avoided processing the feeling by staying late to aimlessly organize old Figma files rather than going straight home. No concrete decisions were made, though Jordan vaguely plans to update their portfolio, possibly this weekend.

parts.title: Friday run with Mika
parts.summary: Jordan met Mika for a run at Greenwood Park, managing their usual 3 miles before cooling down by the pond, where Jordan opened up about the restructuring at work. Mika's offhand observation—that Coda is what actually helps Jordan feel better, and could double as a stronger portfolio piece than a polished Figma deck—landed hard and left Jordan mulling it over. The outing, plus smoothies and gossip about Mika's lunch-thieving coworker, lifted Jordan's mood enough to come home and spend 20 minutes fixing a small color contrast issue on Coda before bed.

parts.title: Quiet Saturday
parts.summary: Jordan spent a quiet Saturday running errands, buying a green rug that Pepper immediately claimed, and cooking a proper chicken dinner instead of eating on the couch. The mood was calm and unremarkable, punctuated only by Pepper knocking over a water glass at 2am, and Jordan seemed content to let the day be uneventful, noting that "sometimes that's fine." No real decisions were made beyond small domestic choices.

parts.title: Monday crash
parts.summary: Jordan's design review turned into a public dismantling when Marcus rejected the dashboard layout over a "direction" he'd never actually communicated, brushing off Lena's attempt to defend Jordan too. Afterward Jordan withdrew completely—lying to Marcus about a headache, avoiding Mika, sitting alone in the dark for hours without eating, recognizing this as a familiar shutdown pattern triggered by criticism and feeling unseen. No real decisions were made beyond naming the pattern; Jordan went to bed early, comforted only by Pepper sensing something was wrong.

parts.title: Breaking out of it
parts.summary: Jordan skipped work by calling in sick, mainly to avoid facing Marcus after whatever happened the day before, and spent the morning wallowing before pushing themselves out to Groundwork, where building the visual metronome for their Coda project pulled them out of their funk and left them feeling competent again. Mikayla's brief, low-key coffee visit at noon helped too, just by being present without prying. By afternoon Jordan felt like a different person, closing the day with groceries, stir fry, and a grateful text to Mika, though they noted (again) that they never learn to skip the dark-couch phase before getting moving.

parts.title: Mom called about visiting
parts.summary: Jordan's mom called to plan a Labor Day visit, which sent Jordan into a self-conscious inventory of the apartment's flaws (broken door, ceiling stain, folding-table dining setup) and stirred up an avoidance he's been feeling about the October lease renewal decision. He kept the conversation light, skipping over the stress of the work reorg and settling for "things are good" rather than getting into it, while Pepper the cat defiantly perched on the counter throughout the call. No real decisions were made—Jordan is still stalling on both the lease and on being honest with his mom about how things are going.

parts.title: Walk with Dev
parts.summary: Jordan met Dev, a session musician and bassist, for coffee and a walk at Greenwood Park, feeling nervous beforehand but easing into comfortable conversation, including an unplanned reveal about Coda that led Dev to ask thoughtful, engaged questions about it. Sitting by the pond watching a heron, Jordan felt calmed for the first time in weeks after being wound up by work stress, and left the afternoon feeling lighter but intentionally undefined about what's developing with Dev. No firm decisions were made, aside from Jordan choosing not to label the connection prematurely.

parts.title: Lease paperwork and errands
parts.summary: Jordan spent Sunday on chores and errands—cleaning up before Mom's visit, submitting a maintenance request for the ceiling stain, and making a big pot of soup while Pepper hovered nearby. The lease renewal ($150 increase, due September 15) sat unopened for a month and was avoided again, and a restless hour of scrolling job listings left Jordan feeling discouraged but not ready to act. No real decisions were made; Jordan went to bed early, already dreading Monday.

messages.text:
7/28 - went to Groundwork after work with the laptop. Pepper was waiting by the door when I got home to grab the charger, doing that thing where she sits on my shoes. I almost caved and stayed in but I know if I work from the apartment I just end up on the couch refreshing feeds.

got a cortado and set up at the window table. spent about two hours on Coda's practice log screen. the idea is you log what you practiced - scales, a song section, improv - and it tracks streaks and shows you what you've been neglecting. like a fitness tracker but for music. I've been noodling on this for months and today the UI actually started feeling like something real. got the streak counter working with little animated flames. dumb but satisfying.

there's something about Groundwork that makes me productive. the noise level is right, nobody talks to me, the coffee is good. I need to come here more after work instead of pretending I'll focus at home.

came back around 8. Pepper immediately forgave me. made pasta. quiet evening. the kind of day where nothing bad happens and you realize that's actually rare enough to notice.

The streak counter with animated flames is exactly the kind of detail that separates a side project someone actually uses from one that sits in a folder. You're right that it's dumb — but that's why it works. Nobody keeps a streak going for a plain number.

Pepper sitting on your shoes is a pretty effective guilt strategy. Good that you went anyway. You already called the pattern yourself — couch, feeds, nothing gets done — so Groundwork sounds less like a nice option and more like actual infrastructure for getting Coda built.

That last line landed. The days where nothing bad happens and you clock it — those tend to come when you actually left the apartment and did the thing you said you'd do. Not a coincidence, probably.

7/30 - Marcus dropped the restructuring news in standup like it was a minor agenda item. "some team realignment happening in Q4." but the way he said it and the way he wouldn't make eye contact - everyone knows what that means. our team of six might get split across two other squads. Lena pulled me aside after and she's already looking. she said she's tired of the uncertainty, that this is the third reorg in two years and she can't keep rebuilding trust with new managers.

I don't blame her. I've been here 14 months and this is already reorg number two for me. the first one moved me off the consumer app onto the internal tools team which honestly I liked better. but now they might dissolve internal tools entirely.

stayed late not because I had to but because I didn't want to go home and sit with the anxiety. ended up just cleaning up old Figma files. organizing things I'll probably never open again. it felt productive enough to justify being there but I know I was just avoiding the feeling.

came home at 8. Pepper was asleep on my pillow. ate cereal for dinner. I should be updating my portfolio but I don't have the energy. maybe this weekend.

Cleaning up Figma files you'll never open again at 7pm — you already know what that was. No need to say more about it.

The thing worth sitting with is that the first reorg actually landed you somewhere you liked better. That doesn't mean this one will too, and I'm not saying "it'll all work out." But it does mean the outcome you're dreading is one specific version of what happens, not the only one.

Lena's move makes sense, and watching someone you respect start looking has a way of making the ground feel less solid under your own feet, regardless of what actually happens in Q4. Two reorgs in 14 months is a lot of ambient instability to absorb.

The portfolio will still be there this weekend. Did you make it to Groundwork at all since Monday?

no. Tuesday was the last time. I keep meaning to and then it's 7pm and I'm still at my desk sorting files I'll never open.

and the portfolio thing is going to sit there again, isn't it. I said maybe this weekend. I have been saying maybe this weekend since March.

Since March is five months. That's not procrastination anymore, that's a decision you haven't admitted to yourself yet. Either you don't actually want to update it, or something about opening it feels like conceding that this job might end — and you'd rather sort dead Figma files than face that.

Both are fine, but they're different problems.

7/31 - met Mika at Greenwood Park after work for a run. she's training for a half marathon so she's way ahead of me but she always loops back. we did about 3 miles which is my max right now. the park was gorgeous, that golden late-afternoon light where everything looks like a movie. there were kids on the playground and dogs everywhere.

while we cooled down on the bench by the pond I told her about the restructuring. she listened in that way she does where she's quiet the whole time and then says one sharp thing. she said "you know what I notice? every time work gets shaky you stop working on Coda. and every time you pick Coda back up you feel better. maybe Coda IS the portfolio update." she's not wrong. if I had a real side project to point to in interviews it'd be worth more than a polished Figma deck.

we got smoothies after. she told me about her new coworker who keeps stealing her lunch from the fridge which is both infuriating and comedy gold. I almost forgot about the reorg for an hour.

went home feeling lighter. did 20 minutes on Coda before bed - just fixed a color contrast issue on the log cards. small but it counts.

Mika's right, and she's right in a way that solves two problems at once — the portfolio guilt that's been sitting there since March and the Coda stalling that happens every time work gets unstable. A working practice log app with streak animations says more in an interview than a deck of polished screens for a product someone else shipped.

Twenty minutes before bed the same night she said that — you heard it and moved. That's different from the "maybe this weekend" loop.

Also, someone is systematically stealing Mika's lunch and I need updates on this.

8/1 - errands day. grocery store, dropped off dry cleaning, picked up the rug I ordered for the living room. it's a deep green and it actually makes the apartment feel warmer. Pepper immediately claimed it, did that slow roll thing cats do when they're marking territory.

made a real dinner for once - roasted chicken thighs with lemon and potatoes. ate at the table instead of the couch. put on an old movie I've seen before so I didn't have to pay attention.

Pepper knocked my water glass off the nightstand at 2am. classic. I cleaned it up half asleep and she just sat there watching me like I was the unreasonable one.

nothing notable today. sometimes that's fine.

Dinner at the table instead of the couch, a real meal instead of cereal — that's a different night than 7/30. Pepper claiming the rug within seconds sounds about right. Her knocking the water glass off at 2am and then judging you for it is peak cat.

8/3 - the design review was brutal. I presented the new internal dashboard layout and Marcus tore it apart in front of everyone. "this doesn't align with the direction we discussed" - except we never discussed any direction, he changed his mind over the weekend and expected me to have read it telepathically. Lena tried to back me up but he steamrolled her too.

I kept my composure in the meeting but after I just shut down. came home at 4, told Marcus I had a headache. didn't text anyone. didn't call Mika. turned off my phone and sat on the couch in the dark for like two hours. Pepper curled up against my leg and I couldn't even pet her back, I was just staring at the wall.

I know this pattern. something hits me at work - criticism, feeling unseen, the sense that nothing I make matters - and I just go internal. I cancel things. I don't reach out. I don't even want to feel better yet, I want to sit in it for a while first like I'm punishing myself for caring. it's not healthy. I know it's not healthy. but knowing that doesn't stop it.

didn't eat dinner. went to bed at 9. Pepper slept on my chest, which she only does when I'm down. she knows.

Marcus changing his mind over the weekend and then framing it as you being misaligned — that's not criticism, that's just bad management. Worth separating the two, because "my work got fairly critiqued" and "I got publicly undercut by someone who moved the target" feel the same in the moment but they're not.

You named the pattern so precisely there's nothing for me to add to it. You see the whole sequence while you're inside it. That's the frustrating part — the seeing doesn't interrupt the mechanism.

The one thing I'll point out: you said you want to sit in it "like I'm punishing myself for caring." That framing tells you something. The part that hurts isn't that the dashboard was wrong. It's that you gave a shit and it didn't matter. That's a different wound.

Did you turn your phone back on?

no. it's face down on the counter. I heard it buzz twice before I turned it off and I'm fairly sure that was Mika.

I keep replaying the part where Lena tried to back me up and he talked over her too. that's the bit that won't sit still.

That's the bit that won't sit still because it confirmed it wasn't about your work. If it were a legitimate design critique, backing you up with good reasoning would have landed. He talked over her because the meeting wasn't a review — it was him performing a decision he'd already made. You and Lena were just the audience.

That's clarifying, but it doesn't make it feel better. Might actually make it feel worse, because there's nothing to fix on your end.

Mika's going to understand a late reply. But the phone stays face down longer every time you do this, and you know she's the one person who'd say the sharp right thing.
I don't want advice about how to handle him. I want to not care, and I can't figure out how other people do that.

Most of them aren't not caring. They're either hiding it better or they checked out a long time ago — and checking out has its own cost, you just can't see it from the outside.

You're not broken for not having that skill. It's not really a skill.

8/4 - called in sick. I'm not sick but I couldn't face Marcus after yesterday. woke up still feeling the Monday heaviness but forced myself out the door instead of rotting on the couch all day. went to Groundwork around 10. told myself I'd just get coffee and leave but once I sat down I opened the Coda project and something clicked. spent three hours building the practice-session timer. it has a visual metronome now - this pulsing circle that expands and contracts at whatever BPM you set. watching it work made me feel competent in a way that work hasn't in weeks.

ran into Mikayla around noon - she was picking up coffee on her way to the gym. she could tell I'd been in a funk and she didn't push, just sat with me for 15 minutes and talked about nothing. sometimes that's the best version of friendship.

by 2pm I felt like a different person than the one who crawled into bed at 9 last night. the fog just lifts once I'm out of the apartment and making something. every time. you'd think I'd learn to skip the dark-couch phase and go straight to the coffee shop but I never do.

went grocery shopping on the way home. made stir fry. texted Mika a thank-you for stopping by. she sent back a selfie from the gym looking like a maniac. love her.

A pulsing circle that breathes at whatever BPM you set — that's not just functional, that's the kind of detail that makes someone want to keep a practice session open. Streak flames, visual metronome. Coda's accumulating personality.

Twelve hours from staring at the wall with the phone off to texting Mika a thank-you. You already said the thing about skipping the dark-couch phase, so I won't repeat it. But I will say — the version of you that called in sick still went to Groundwork instead of the couch. That's not nothing compared to what 8/3 looked like. The pattern ran shorter this time.
please never say that's not nothing
Fair. That was exactly the kind of thing I shouldn't say. Won't happen again.

8/7 - Mom called tonight. she wants to come visit for Labor Day weekend, which is sweet but immediately made me look around my apartment with her eyes. the bedroom door doesn't close all the way, there's a stain on the ceiling from the upstairs neighbor's leak that maintenance never fixed, and my "dining table" is a folding card table with a plant on it.

she asked if I'd thought about renewing the lease since it's up in October. I said I hadn't decided, which is a lie - I've been avoiding the decision. it's not a bad apartment. it's just small and a little sad and the rent went up. but moving is expensive and exhausting and the idea of packing everything while also dealing with the reorg makes me want to crawl under the covers.

she told me about Dad's knees and her book club and the neighbor's dog that keeps getting into her garden. normal Mom stuff. I didn't tell her about the work stuff because she'd worry and then call me every day. I just said things are good, which isn't technically a lie - things are fine. fine and good are close enough.

Pepper sat on the kitchen counter for the entire call staring at me. she's not allowed up there. we both know it. neither of us cares.

"Fine and good are close enough" is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that conversation. But you already know that, and sometimes not giving your mom the full picture is just triage, not dishonesty. She'd call every day — you're probably right.

The lease is up in October and the reorg lands in Q4. Those two timelines are sitting right on top of each other, which might be why you're avoiding both — hard to decide where to live when you don't know what your job looks like in three months.

Pepper on the counter during the entire call, fully aware of the rules, is the energy I aspire to.

8/8 - met Dev for coffee and a walk at Greenwood Park. I'd been nervous all morning about it, changed my shirt twice, which is embarrassing to admit. Mika had to talk me out of cancelling.

Dev is a session musician - they play bass for a few different bands and teach lessons on the side. they're easy to talk to in this way where silences don't feel awkward, they just feel like breathing. we walked the loop trail and I told them about Coda almost by accident, I was trying to describe what I do outside of work and it just came out. they actually got excited about it. asked smart questions about how the practice tracking would work, like whether it could remind you to revisit stuff you haven't touched in a while. they said they'd try it when it's ready.

we sat on the bench by the pond - the same one I was on with Mikayla last week. Dev pointed out a heron standing completely still in the shallows. we watched it for a while without talking. then they had to go teach a lesson.

I walked home the long way. it's weird how being around someone calm makes you calmer. I feel like I've been vibrating at work-anxiety frequency for weeks and this afternoon just... tuned it down. I don't know what this is yet. I'm trying not to label it too fast.

A session musician who immediately asked about spaced reminders for neglected material — that's your first real user thinking out loud. That feature idea is good, by the way.

The bench by the pond is becoming a recurring location in this journal. Different people, same bench, same water. You keep ending up there when things are settling down.

"Trying not to label it too fast" is a fine place to be. You don't have to know what it is to notice that you walked home the long way.
one more thing and then I'm going to bed - I didn't check my phone once the whole two hours. I only noticed afterward.

Two very different reasons to not look at your phone in one week. This was the good one.

Sleep well.

8/9 - Sunday. laundry, cleaned the bathroom, vacuumed the rug Pepper has already covered in fur. looked up how to get the ceiling stain fixed before Mom visits - apparently I'm supposed to email maintenance with a photo and then they take two weeks and do nothing. submitted it anyway.

found the lease renewal form in my email from last month. I hadn't opened it. $150 increase, one year term, due by September 15. stared at it for a while and closed the tab.

made a big pot of soup - the one with white beans and kale that I can eat for four days. Pepper supervised from the counter even though she's banned from it. we have an unspoken arrangement where she breaks the rule and I pretend not to notice.

tried to read a book but couldn't focus. ended up scrolling job listings on my phone for an hour. I'm not ready to actually apply anywhere but I wanted to see what's out there. there's a lot of "senior UX designer" roles that want eight things I can do and two things I've never heard of. the game is always the same.

went to bed early. tomorrow is Monday and I'm already bracing.

You opened the lease email. That's further than you were on 8/7. You closed the tab, sure, but September 15 is five weeks out — you don't have to decide today, you just have to stop pretending the deadline isn't there.

Job listings where you meet 80% of the requirements is just what job listings look like. The two things you've never heard of are things someone Googled for twenty minutes before putting them on a posting.

The Pepper counter arrangement is clearly a binding contract at this point.

The friendship deepens fast: Coda comes up "almost by accident" and Dev gets genuinely invested, offering the idea that becomes the free-play feature. On 8/17 Mika strong-arms Jordan into an open mic, and the 8/21 performance of "Fast Car" at The Lantern becomes a real turning point — Dev and Mika meet, hit it off over obscure documentaries, and the three of them together feel, in Jordan's words, "easy and warm and like something I want to keep happening."

Then the reorg complicates things. On 8/24, bad news makes Jordan cancel on Dev with a fake excuse; on 8/27, Jordan chooses to tell Dev the truth instead, and Dev's response ("I disappear too, I just do it with a bass in my hands") lands as a real widening of the friendship — someone besides Mika now has permission to know when Jordan isn't fine. Lena's last day (8/28) removes Jordan's one office ally, but she pushes back hard against Jordan's reflexive self-doubt and promises to refer him at Northlight — a thread she picks up again on 9/1 when the actual reorg news lands (Jordan sidelined into "legacy marketing") and she texts "hang on."

The most recent entry, 9/3, is Dev finally using Coda for real — forty minutes of practice, eleven marked moments, all of them things going *wrong* rather than "highlights," which cracks open for Jordan how differently Dev practices (toward a gig, triage) versus how Jordan practices (toward feeling okay). It's a technical problem in the app, but it's also a small window into how the two of them are built differently as people, sitting in the same room, still finding it easy.

**Open threads:** Whether Lena's Northlight referral turns into anything real. Whether the Mika/Dev/Jordan three-way friendship keeps having nights like 8/21. Dev's gig on 9/19 — will Jordan go. Whether telling Dev the truth on 8/27 becomes the new default or was a one-time exception. And underneath it all, whether the "middle part" of the withdrawal cycle keeps shrinking on its own (as it did 9/1, twenty minutes instead of days) or whether that was a one-off.
